items.followUp: What is a hypothesis? Name the two types of data used in biological observations.

rubric.description: Defines observation as noticing and recording facts or events, using senses or instruments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition’s central idea; accept equivalent wording involving careful watching and recording evidence.
Award 1 mark only when both types are named.

modelAnswer: An observation is the careful noting and recording of facts or events, using the senses or instruments.
The two types of observations are qualitative and quantitative.

items.followUp: State two observations that led scientists to investigate the role of mosquitoes in spreading malaria.

rubric.why: Recognises the reported association between malaria and places where mosquitoes were plentiful.
rubric.description: States that malaria was common in areas where mosquitoes were abundant, such as marshy areas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation or an equivalent statement linking malaria prevalence with abundant mosquitoes.

rubric.why: Gives another observation supporting an association between mosquito exposure and malaria.
rubric.description: States that malaria was more likely among people sleeping outdoors or near open windows, or that malaria outbreaks coincided with the mosquito season.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one distinct observation of this kind.

modelAnswer: A.F.A. King observed that malaria was common in places where mosquitoes were abundant, such as marshy areas.
He also observed that people sleeping outdoors or near open windows were more likely to suffer from malaria.

items.followUp: Define magnification and state what is meant by resolving power.

rubric.why: States how magnification compares an image with the actual object.
rubric.description: Defines magnification as the number of times the image is larger than the actual object, or the ratio of image size to actual size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the comparison or ratio.

rubric.why: Captures the ability of a microscope to distinguish nearby details.
rubric.description: Defines resolving power as the ability to distinguish two very close points or objects as separate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the ability to resolve close points as distinct.

modelAnswer: Magnification is the number of times an image is larger than the actual object (image size ÷ actual size).
Resolving power is the ability to distinguish two very close points as separate.

items.followUp: What happens to a plant cell placed in a hypotonic solution? Explain by referring to water movement.

rubric.why: Defines a hypertonic solution relative to the cell.
rubric.description: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell contents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the relative concentration.

rubric.why: Defines a hypotonic solution relative to the cell.
rubric.description: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell contents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the relative concentration.

modelAnswer: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell contents.
A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell contents.

items.followUp: What is a tetrad, and when does crossing over occur during meiosis?

rubric.why: Identifies chiasmata as visible contact points between homologous chromosomes.
rubric.description: Chiasmata are the points where homologous chromosomes remain attached after crossing over.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the contact or attachment points.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the exchange process from the points where it is visible.
rubric.description: Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the exchange of chromatid segments.

modelAnswer: Chiasmata are the points of attachment between homologous chromosomes where crossing over has occurred.
Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.

items.followUp: How do malignant tumours differ from benign tumours in their growth and spread?

rubric.why: States the invasive or spreading nature of malignant tumours.
rubric.description: Malignant tumours invade nearby tissues and can spread to other parts of the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for invasion or spread beyond the original site.

rubric.why: Contrasts the limited growth of benign tumours with malignant spread.
rubric.description: Benign tumours remain localized and do not invade or spread to other parts of the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that benign tumours do not invade or spread.

modelAnswer: Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissues and may spread to other parts of the body.
Benign tumours remain localized and do not invade or spread to other parts of the body.

items.followUp: What are genes, and where are they found in a cell?

rubric.why: Gives the characteristic structure of chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their thread-like form.

rubric.why: Identifies their location and genetic material.
rubric.description: Chromosomes are found in the nucleus and consist of DNA associated with proteins; they carry genes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly locating chromosomes in the nucleus and linking them to DNA or genes.

modelAnswer: Chromosomes are thread-like structures found in the nucleus of a cell.
They consist of DNA associated with proteins and carry genes.

items.followUp: Where are photosystems found, and what role do they perform in photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Identifies the pigment-and-protein components of a photosystem.
rubric.description: A photosystem is a group of chlorophyll and accessory pigment molecules associated with proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the pigment-protein group.

rubric.why: States the location or light-capturing role of a photosystem.
rubric.description: Photosystems are in the thylakoid membranes and absorb or trap light energy for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the location or light-capturing role.

modelAnswer: A photosystem is a group of chlorophyll and accessory pigment molecules associated with proteins.
Photosystems are present in the thylakoid membranes, where they capture light energy for photosynthesis.
